questions.q: Why can both a too-small and a too-large learning rate produce the same visual symptom of a 'flat' loss curve?
options: They can't -- only a too-small learning rate causes a flat-looking curve
A too-small LR moves the loss so slowly it looks flat, while a too-large LR causes the loss to bounce around a region without making net progress, which can also look flat on a chart
A too-large learning rate always causes an immediate crash, not a plateau
Learning rate has no effect on whether a loss curve looks flat
questions.explain: Both extremes can produce a loss curve that fails to show clear downward progress, for opposite underlying reasons -- which is why a quick LR sweep across orders of magnitude is the cheapest first check.

questions.q: What does it mean if the training loss is clearly decreasing but the tracked evaluation metric stays flat?
options: The model is definitely broken and needs more capacity
The loss being optimized and the metric being watched may not be well-correlated, so the apparent plateau in the metric isn't necessarily a training failure
This can never happen -- loss and metric always move together
The learning rate must be set too high
questions.explain: A loss/metric mismatch (e.g. optimizing per-token cross-entropy while watching sequence-level exact match) can make the metric look stuck even though the model is learning something, as measured by the loss.

questions.q: Why is checking the label distribution with something like `collections.Counter` a useful step when a run plateaus?
options: It directly measures the model's capacity

It can reveal a label collapse or deduplication bug where the effective dataset has far fewer unique labels or examples than expected, which often explains a plateau better than an architecture problem
It replaces the need for a learning-rate sweep entirely
It only matters for regression tasks, never classification
questions.explain: A near-total collapse onto one label, or an accidentally deduplicated dataset, is a data bug that can produce a stubborn plateau -- and it's a one-line, seconds-long check, far cheaper than redesigning the architecture.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend checking learning rate, loss/metric alignment, and data issues before considering a model-capacity problem?
options: Because capacity problems are impossible in modern architectures
Because those checks are much cheaper to rule out (minutes or seconds) than the most expensive hypothesis to test, which is redesigning or substantially resizing the architecture
Because data issues are the only possible cause of a plateau
Because learning rate is always the correct explanation
questions.explain: The suggested order follows cost: an LR sweep and a label-distribution check are cheap and fast, while testing a capacity hypothesis (e.g. substantially increasing model size) is the most expensive, so it's checked last.

questions.q: What is one way to test whether a model genuinely lacks the capacity to solve a task, as opposed to having an optimization problem?
options: Running the exact same architecture for a longer number of epochs
Substantially increasing model size on a small subset of data and checking whether the plateau moves
Lowering the learning rate further
Switching from fp32 to fp16 training
questions.explain: If a substantially larger model on a small subset still can't move past the plateau, that points toward a genuine capacity or representation problem rather than an optimization issue like learning rate.
